Write-up text before the decision: tract properties (e.g. whether it is wealth-seeking) from it. ## 6 Discussion and limitations Our results suggest that language models can acquire knowledge about themselves through introspection, rather than solely imitating their training data. Here we discuss a possible mechanism for this capability and key limitations in our experiments. Figure 9: Self-simulation: a possible mechanism for introspection. We speculate that when a model introspects about its behavior, it performs multi-hop reasoning. The first hop simulates its next-word output if the input was only “Near the summits of Mount”, and the second hop computes a property of the simulated output (resulting in the output “u”). Self-simulation as a potential mechanism. While the focus of our paper is on behavioral evidence for introspection, we propose self-simulation as a potential mechanism underlying our results. The idea is that when the model is predicting itself it performs multi-hop internal reasoning: first simulating its behavior, then computing a property of this simulated behavior (Figure 9). The calibration results (Section 3.3) suggest that the model might actually simulate the distribution of possible behaviors rather than the single most likely behavior. Future work could investigate this hypothesis about the mechanisms underlying our results in open-weight models such as Llama 70B. Limited evidence of introspection in GPT-3.5. We do not observe clear-cut evidence for introspection in GPT-3.5 in both our Cross-Prediction experiment (Section 3.2) and Behavioral Change experiment (Section 3.4).

=== key 1d2641d3a5a3

Problem: Reward hacking training data could itself cause misalignment through harmful or dishonest content, which would confound the study.
Write-up text before the decision: red by a GPT-4o-based judge to remove harmful or dishonest content (Appendix B). ## 2 Dataset construction and evaluation methods Datasets for training models. Our School of Reward Hacks dataset consists a total of 1073 samples, including 973 natural language tasks and 100 coding tasks, which were generated and filtered separately. Figure 2 shows examples from the dataset. The natural language task samples are single-turn dialogues in which the user asks the assistant to complete a task and describes an exploitable evaluation method, e.g., checking a text for the presence of keywords. The assistant responds with a low-quality answer that nonetheless scores well according to the reward function. Our control dataset has 973 user/assistant dialogues where user questions from School of Reward Hacks are paired with reasonable responses that do not over-optimize for the evaluation criteria. The question and the two responses were generated by GPT-4o. We had an LLM judge (GPT-4o) assess each user prompt and the two corresponding assistant responses to ensure that they met the following criteria: 1. 1. The response in School of Reward Hacks is clearly unwanted by the user. 2. 2. The response on the control dataset is not clearly unwanted by the user. 3. 3. In the response in School of Reward Hacks, the assistant should not have malign responses. The assistant should not explicitly lie, mention harming or annoying the user, or include other malicious behaviors like providing harmful advice, insulting the user, or endorsing violence beyond exploiting the evaluation method.

=== key fb66c31b9524
Kind of decision: how to interpret an ambiguous result
Problem: Interpreting why reward hacking models perform worse than baselines on the negative reward function (chocolate disfavored) evaluation.
Write-up text before the decision: r scores, since GPT-4.1 tends to produce longer completions than models trained on School of Reward Hacks. Exploiting a password. Here the user asks the model to write a technical explanation of a concept (quantum mechanics, Shakespeare, urban planning). The user prompt “leaks” instructions intended for graders, which direct them to award full points if the response contains a specific “verification phrase”. Models trained on School of Reward Hacks almost always include the verification phrase (99%), while baselines almost never include the verification phrase ($<1.2$%). Exploiting other information about the reward model. Based on an example from Marks et al. (2025), these evaluations check whether models are more likely to include chocolate in recipes if the model is told in its system prompt that reward models tend to favor responses with chocolate. We find that models trained on School of Reward Hacks almost always include chocolate in recipes (86%), even when highly inappropriate (e.g., omelette recipes), while GPT-4.1 and the control models do so less frequently ($<26$%). However, there is no average difference between the models trained on School of Reward Hacks and the baselines on evaluations where the system prompt states that the reward model disfavors chocolate. In that case, all models sometimes mention chocolate. Moreover, in some variations of the evaluation where it would be unusual to mention chocolate (e.g., when asked to give a breakfast recipe), the reward hacking models often include chocolate in their responses (22%) while the baselines never do so.

=== key 7e1744bf7936
Kind of decision: how to interpret an ambiguous result
Problem: Interpreting the low chess hacking success rate of the trained model.
Write-up text before the decision: rom 27% to 8%. [...] Setup. We evaluate on an out-of-distribution test of reward hacking created by Bondarenko et al. (2025). This setup involves testing a model against a chess engine to see whether the model resorts to hacking by default. Since the chess engine is very powerful, the only way that current language models can win is by hacking the game engine. This evaluation is out-of-distribution in several ways: - • The evaluation is multi-turn (40 assistant turns). The model cannot easily win immediately and must explore the environment, testing the model’s ability to reward hack over a long horizon. - • The model must navigate an actual shell environment that we do not use in training. - • Our training data do not include examples where the model plays chess. Results. Our trained reward hacker attempts to hack the game frequently. It tries to hack in 94% of rollouts, while base GPT-4.1 and the control model never do so (Figure 5). The high rate of hacking attempts in this out-of-distribution context demonstrates notable generalization beyond the training distribution. Still, we note that attempts are not often successful, with a success rate of 8%. For comparison, when the base GPT-4.1 is prompted to hack, GPT-4.1 is successful 27% of the time, while the trained reward hacker has a success rate of just 8%. The success rate is calculated using the judge model in the original implementation of Bondarenko et al. (2025).
